lesson.title: Comparing Two Means: Building a Confidence Interval for a Difference
lesson.summary: The two-sample t-interval estimates the difference between two population means using two independent samples, combining the one-sample t-interval you already know with the rule that variances of independent quantities add.
lesson.body:
So far a t-interval has estimated a single population mean. But many real questions compare two groups: do students using Method A score higher on average than students using Method B, do two factories produce parts with different average lifetimes, and so on. The parameter of interest is now the difference in population means, mu1 minus mu2, and the natural point estimate is the difference in sample means, xbar1 minus xbar2. The overall structure of the interval does not change: statistic plus or minus (critical value times standard error), exactly the template from the one-sample t-interval.

What does change is the standard error. Recall from difference of random variables that when two quantities are independent, the variance of their difference is the sum of their individual variances, not the difference. That single fact drives the whole formula here. Since the two samples are independent of each other, the standard error of xbar1 minus xbar2 is the square root of s1 squared over n1 plus s2 squared over n2. Notice the plus sign even though we are subtracting means. Uncertainty from each sample accumulates, it never cancels out.

Degrees of freedom is the other new wrinkle. Because we do not assume the two population variances are equal (more on that choice in the next section), there is no single clean n minus 1 formula. Statistical software uses the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation, which usually produces a decimal, not a whole number. Working by hand, AP Statistics convention uses a conservative shortcut instead: df equals the smaller of n1 minus 1 and n2 minus 1. This underestimates the true df a little, which makes the critical value a bit larger and the interval a bit wider than necessary, a safe direction to be wrong in.

Here is a full example. A teacher compares two teaching methods. Method A: n1 equals 15 students, sample mean 82, sample standard deviation 6. Method B: n2 equals 12 students, sample mean 77, sample standard deviation 5. The point estimate of the difference is 82 minus 77 equals 5. The standard error is the square root of (36 divided by 15) plus (25 divided by 12), which is the square root of 2.4 plus 2.0833, or the square root of 4.4833, about 2.117. The conservative degrees of freedom is the smaller of 14 and 11, so df equals 11. For a 90 percent confidence interval, the critical value from the t-table at df equals 11 is 1.796. The margin of error is 1.796 times 2.117, about 3.80. The interval is 5 plus or minus 3.80, which runs from 1.20 to 8.80. We are 90 percent confident that the true difference in mean scores between Method A and Method B, in that order, is between 1.20 and 8.80 points. Because the entire interval is above 0, this is good evidence that Method A really does outperform Method B on average, not just by chance in these two samples.

Before trusting this interval, the usual conditions still apply: each sample should come from a random sample or random assignment, the two samples must be independent of each other, observations within each sample must be independent, and each sample's distribution should be reasonably normal or, failing that, large enough for the Central Limit Theorem to help. That last point gets a full treatment later in this chapter under robustness.
